objectives.label: Resources of collecting data
objectives.description: Distinguish primary resources from secondary resources of collecting data and state the advantages of each.

objectives.label: Methods of collecting data
objectives.description: Identify the method of collecting data (method of mass population or method of samples) suited to the aim and size of the statistical society, stating its advantages and disadvantages.

objectives.label: Selecting types of samples
objectives.description: Select a sample using a biased choice, a simple random sample or a layer sample, and decide how many units to take from each layer.

entries.text: Secondary resources (historical resources): we can get data from authorities and agencies that formally work, such as the central agency for mobilization and statistics, internet and media. This type is a good type of resource because it saves time and money.

A.why: Defines secondary resources and their advantage.

B.why: Defines secondary resources and their advantage.

entries.text: Picture of a woman seated at a computer showing a bar chart on the screen; illustrates secondary resources.

A.why: Illustrates secondary resources.

B.why: Illustrates secondary resources of data.

entries.text: Photo of a crowd of school students; illustrates a statistical society.

A.why: Statistical society picture introduces the methods of collecting data from a society.

B.why: Illustrates a statistical society, the basis for choosing a collection method.

entries.text: Clip-art picture of people with a telescope/survey scene and a woman at a computer; illustrates the method of mass population.

A.why: Illustrates the method of mass population.

B.why: Illustrates the method of mass population.

entries.text: Advantage 1: using samples saves time, efforts and money.

A.why: Advantage of the sample method.

B.why: Advantage of the sample method: saves time, effort and money.

entries.text: Advantage 2: it is the only way to collect data about gigantic societies (like fish).

A.why: Advantage of samples for gigantic societies.

B.why: Advantage of the sample method for gigantic societies.

entries.text: Advantage 3: it is the only method to study some limited societies, such as the two cases below.

A.why: Advantage of samples for some limited societies.

B.why: Advantage of the sample method for some limited societies.

entries.text: A: Check the patient's blood by getting a sample (checking the whole blood leads to death).

A.why: Case showing samples are the only way (blood test).

B.why: Blood test is a case where only a sample can be used, an advantage of samples.

entries.text: B: Check the production of a factory producing electric lamps to determine the validity of the lamp (know for how long the lamp can be used before getting burned).

A.why: Case showing samples are the only way (lamp production).

B.why: Lamp testing is a case where only a sample can be used, an advantage of samples.

entries.text: A disadvantage of sample methods: outcomes are not accurate if the selected sample doesn't represent all the society well; in such a case the sample is called biased.

A.why: Disadvantage of the sample method.

B.why: States a disadvantage of the sample method of collecting data.

entries.text: Biased selection means selecting the sample in a way to satisfy the objectives of the research; this is called a deliberate sample.

A.why: Defines biased selection, a way to select a sample.

B.why: Defines biased (deliberate) selection of a sample.

entries.text: Random selection means selecting a sample such that the chance of getting any value from the society is equal.

A.why: Defines random selection of a sample.

B.why: Defines random selection, used for simple random samples.

entries.text: 1. Simple random sample: the simplest type of sample; it can be got from homogeneous societies where selection is related to the size and number of units in the society.

A.why: Defines the simple random sample.

B.why: Defines the simple random sample type.

entries.text: A. If the size of the society is small: when choosing 5 students of a 40-student class, prepare an identical card for each student with name or number, put them in a box, draw a card randomly and return it again; repeat until the sample needed is obtained.

A.why: How to draw a simple random sample from a small society.

B.why: Card-drawing method for a random sample from a small society.

entries.text: If the size of the society is big (e.g. selecting a sample of 5 students from 800): number the students from 1 to 800, then use the calculator or Excel to give 10 random digits in the field from 0.000 to 0.999, remove the decimal point so the field runs from zero to 999, and discard the digits that are more than 800.

A.why: How to draw a simple random sample from a big society.

B.why: Selecting a random sample from a big society using calculator or Excel random digits.

entries.text: Calculator key sequence after 'start': ON, SHIFT, Ran# (the dot key), = keys, then a calculator display showing 'Ran #' and 0.624.

A.why: Calculator steps for generating random numbers.

B.why: Calculator Ran# keys show how to generate random numbers for a simple random sample.

entries.text: Five non-repeated digits are enough to give the numbers of the sample of students.

A.why: Says how many digits are needed for the random sample.

B.why: Digits needed to number a random sample is part of drawing a simple random sample.

objectives.label: Range as dispersion
objectives.description: Calculate the range of a set of values (greatest value minus smallest value) and use it, with the mean, to compare the dispersion of two sets.

objectives.label: Standard deviation of values
objectives.description: Calculate the standard deviation of a set of values using the mean and the squared deviations from the mean.

objectives.label: Standard deviation of frequency distributions
objectives.description: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of a frequency distribution, including grouped sets using the centres of the sets.

objectives.label: Compare homogeneity by standard deviation
objectives.description: Decide which of two distributions is more homogeneous by comparing their standard deviations (the larger standard deviation is more dispersed), representing them with a frequency polygon.

entries.text: You have previously learned the central tendency (mean - domain - mode) and used them to calculate a set of data to identify one value describing the trend of these data in centeralization around this value.

A.why: Central tendency is assumed from earlier lessons.

B.why: Recalls previously learned central tendency.

entries.text: The mean = (total of these values) / (their number). $\text{The mean}=\dfrac{\text{Total of these values}}{\text{Their number}}$

A.why: The mean formula is recalled prior knowledge.

B.why: Mean formula is assumed prior knowledge.

entries.text: The dispersion is small if the differences between the values are little, whereas the dispersion is great if the differences between the values are very big.

A.why: Describes small and great dispersion, opening the range idea.

B.why: Small or great dispersion according to differences between values.

entries.text: When the dispersion is zero, all the values are equal.

A.why: Zero dispersion means equal values, part of the dispersion concept.

B.why: Zero dispersion means equal values, part of the dispersion idea with the range.

entries.text: The dispersion is a measure that expresses how homogeneous the sets are.

A.why: Dispersion measures homogeneity, introduced with range.

B.why: Defines dispersion as a measure of homogeneity, in the range introduction.

entries.text: To compare two or more sets of data, we must have a measure of central tendency and another measure of dispersion for each set.

A.why: Compare sets using mean and a dispersion measure, as with range.

B.why: Comparing sets needs mean and a dispersion measure such as the range.

entries.text: The range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value in the set.

A.why: Defines the range.

B.why: Defines the range as greatest minus smallest value.

entries.text: (1) The range is the simplest and easiest method of measuring dispersion.

A.why: Property of the range.

B.why: Range is the simplest measure of dispersion.

entries.text: (2) The range is influenced greatly by the outlier. The values of the second set disperse in a range of 50; when the last value (92) is removed the range = 52 - 42 = 10, or 1/5 of the previous range. $52-42=10=\frac{1}{5}\times 50$

A.why: Range is affected by an outlier.

B.why: Drawback of the range: greatly influenced by the outlier.

entries.text: (3) The range is not influenced by any value in the set except the greatest and smallest values, so it does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of the set.

A.why: Range limitation, depends only on greatest and smallest values.

B.why: Drawback of the range: depends only on greatest and smallest values.

entries.text: Standard deviation is the commonest measure of dispersion and the most accurate (under certain conditions); it is the positive square root of the average of the squared deviations of the values from the mean.

A.why: Defines standard deviation via squared deviations from the mean.

B.why: Defines standard deviation as root of average squared deviations from the mean.

entries.text: Standard deviation σ equals the square root of (the sum of (x − x̄)² divided by n). $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2}{n}}$

A.why: Formula for standard deviation of values.

B.why: Standard deviation formula for a set of values.

entries.text: σ (sigma) denotes the standard deviation of the society (population) of data.

A.why: Symbol σ used in the formula.

B.why: σ notation for standard deviation.

entries.text: x̄ (x Bar) denotes the mean of the values of the society.

A.why: Symbol x̄ used in the formula.

B.why: x̄ notation used in the standard deviation formula.

entries.text: n denotes the number of values.

A.why: Symbol n used in the formula.

B.why: n notation used in the standard deviation formula.

entries.text: ∑ denotes addition (summation).

A.why: Symbol ∑ used in the formula.

B.why: Σ notation used in the standard deviation formula.

entries.text: Table of values x, deviations from the mean 16, and squared deviations, with Sum row (sum of x = 80, sum of squares = 54); sum cell under x - x̄ is blank. x, x - x̄, (x - x̄)² / 12, 12 - 16 = -4, 16 / 13, 13 - 16 = -3, 9 / 16, 16 - 16 = 0, zero / 18, 18 - 16 = 2, 4 / 21, 21 - 16 = 5, 25 / Sum 80, , 54

A.why: Squared deviations table for 12, 13, 16, 18, 21.

B.why: Deviation table for standard deviation of 12, 13, 16, 18, 21.

entries.text: For any frequency distribution, the standard deviation σ equals the square root of Σ(x - x̄)²k divided by Σk. $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2 k}{\sum k}}$

A.why: Standard deviation formula for frequency distributions.

B.why: Standard deviation formula for any frequency distribution.

entries.text: x represents the value or the center of the set.

A.why: x is the value or centre of the set in the frequency formula.

B.why: x denotes value or centre of set, notation for frequency distributions.

entries.text: k represents the frequency of the value or the set.

A.why: k is frequency in the frequency formula.

B.why: k denotes frequency, notation for frequency distributions.

entries.text: Σk is the total of frequency. $\sum k$

A.why: Σk is total frequency.

B.why: Σk is total frequency, notation for frequency distributions.

entries.text: x̄ is the mean, equal to Σxk divided by Σk. $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum xk}{\sum k}$

A.why: Mean of a frequency distribution.

B.why: Defines the mean of a frequency distribution as Σxk/Σk.

entries.text: First: Set the calculator to the statistical system to enter data (keys On, Mode, 2 (Stat), then 1 (1-VAR); screen shows X and FREQ columns).

A.why: Calculator setup for frequency data entry.

B.why: Setting the calculator to statistics mode for frequency data.

entries.text: Second: Calculate the standard deviation of the frequency distribution (Example 2).

A.why: Calculator σ for a frequency distribution (Example 2).

B.why: Calculator method for the standard deviation of a frequency distribution.

entries.text: Step 1: Enter the centers of sets 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 (keys: On, Mode, 2, 1, then 2 = 6 = 10 = 14 = 18 =).

A.why: Enter centres of sets.

B.why: Enter the centres of the sets on the calculator.

entries.text: Step 2: Go to the top of the second column (FREQ) and enter the corresponding frequency for each set 2, 5, 8, 15, 10.

A.why: Enter frequencies.

B.why: Enter frequencies of the sets on the calculator.

entries.text: Step 4: Go back to the original system and switch off the calculator.

A.why: Final step of the calculator procedure.

B.why: Final calculator step of finding the frequency-distribution standard deviation.

A.why: Calculator screen showing σ ≈ 4.521.

B.why: Calculator screen giving the standard deviation of the frequency distribution.

entries.text: The standard deviation is affected by the deviations of all the values and its value is affected by the outlier.

A.why: Property of standard deviation: uses all deviations, affected by outliers.

B.why: Property of standard deviation: affected by all deviations and by outliers, stated after computing it.

entries.text: The standard deviation has the same measuring units as the original data, so it is used to compare the dispersion of sets which have the same measuring units when the mean is equal. The set which contains more standard deviation is more dispersed.

A.why: Larger standard deviation means more dispersed, used to compare sets.

B.why: States the larger standard deviation means more dispersed, used to compare sets.
